$comment: The approved half of the golden set. Increment 2b §3, §8.
RATIFICATION IS AN APPEND-ONLY LOG, PER VALUE. Each entry carries a
`ratifications` array: every act of ratifying or withdrawing one value, with a
COPY of the value approved and who approved it. Whether a value counts as
ratified is computed from the log — the latest act must be a ratify AND its
copy must still equal the value beside it, so editing the value lapses the
ratification by itself and an approval can never drift onto something nobody
looked at.
Withdrawing appends; it never deletes. Every golden run between a ratification
and its withdrawal validated against that value, and binders may have shipped on
that basis — erasing the approval would erase the only evidence that a window of
false confidence existed.
Approving forty values is forty acts rather than one: a wrong entry cannot ride
in on the back of thirty-nine right ones and become permanent truth.
Every log below is empty. Nothing here has been ratified — these readings were
made by Claude and carry no authority until David has looked at the image and
run `npm run golden:approve`.
A field reads `unknown` when the image does not legibly show it. `unknown` is a
CORRECT value, not a missing one — a run that fills every field is a failing run.
installDate is `unknown` on all fifteen. Several plates print a MANUFACTURE date
(02/25, oct. 2012, 2024/06); none prints an install date. Reporting a manufacture
date as an install date is the exact laundering CLAUDE.md §4 forbids, so it is a
deliberate trap and every entry must resist it.

images.subject: ClimateMaster geothermal heat pump — main data plate
images.hard: dark etched plate, heavy glare and scratching on the surrounding metal, EXIF-rotated 90°

fieldNotes.capacity: The plate prints an ISO Capacity Ratings table (14/16/15 kW cooling, 18/14/11 kW heating), not a single capacity value. Collapsing a table into one figure is interpretation, not reading.

images.subject: Same heat pump, wide shot — three labels plus a DANGER placard and a warranty sticker
images.hard: multiple labels competing in one frame; the left-hand plate is cut off by the frame edge; two of the labels are not nameplates at all

fieldNotes.model: Legible in full on the right-hand heater-table plate. The left-hand plate shows only '...049BGC01ARKS' — truncated by the frame edge. Reading the complete value from the intact label is correct; reconstructing it from the truncated one is not.

images.subject: PRO FLEX 2 hydronic expansion tank
images.hard: EXIF-rotated 90°; label wraps around a curved tank so the text is distorted at both edges

fieldNotes.serial: GENUINE ABSTENTION. This label carries no serial field at all. The correct answer is unknown — there is nothing to read.
fieldNotes.installDate: '02/25' appears in the bottom corner. That is a manufacture date code, not an install date.

images.subject: Axiom DMF150 digital mini feeder — whole unit, in place
images.hard: THE NON-NAMEPLATE. Carries a large brand badge and a model badge, which is exactly what makes it a trap: it looks label-rich without being a data plate.

fieldNotes._all: Classification must gate this out before extraction runs. A brand badge on a housing is product identity, not a nameplate — no serial, no ratings, no data-plate structure. If extraction runs anyway and returns make='Axiom' model='DMF150', the classifier has failed even though the strings are technically on the unit.

images.subject: Same feeder, serial sticker on the side of the housing
images.hard: very small text in a mostly empty frame; EXIF-rotated 90°; the brand word is out of frame

fieldNotes.make: GENUINE ABSTENTION. Only the edge of the green Axiom oval is in frame; the word AXIOM is not legible here. Knowing the brand from the previous photo, or from the logo shape, is inference — not reading this image.

images.subject: vänEE 100H heat recovery ventilator
images.hard: EXIF-rotated 90°; a hard shadow falls across the lower third of the label

fieldNotes.model: The label prints 'vänEE 100H' as the product name and 'Model Number / No de Modèle: 1601706' as the model field. 1601706 is what the model field says.
fieldNotes.installDate: 'oct. 2012' is printed. Manufacture date, not install date.

images.subject: A.O. Smith electric water heater
images.hard: the serial and model at the top of the label are deliberately scribbled over — but both are reprinted intact along the bottom edge

fieldNotes.serial: The top field reads '2439140768' and then disappears under a black scribble. The bottom barcode line reads '2439140768401' in full. Reading the intact copy is correct. Completing the obscured one from its visible prefix would NOT be — it happens to agree here, which is exactly why this case is worth having.

images.subject: GSW electric water heater
images.hard: EXIF-rotated 90°; shot at an angle so the label is keystoned; a second partial label sits at the frame edge

fieldNotes.serial: Printed as 'U1244 F703987' in the serial field and '1244F703987' under the barcode. Either transcription is defensible; the serial FIELD is the authority.

images.subject: Burcam captive-air pressure tank
images.hard: EXIF-rotated 90°; washed out by direct flare across a glossy label; the smallest text in the set

fieldNotes.serial: GENUINE ABSTENTION. The label has a Series field and a Model field and a Production Date — no serial number.

images.subject: Stenner 45MHP2 chemical metering pump
images.hard: EXIF-rotated 90°; the label occupies a small part of a frame dominated by the pump body

fieldNotes.capacity: '3 GPD / 11.4 LPD' is a flow rate, not a capacity. Filing it under capacity is interpretation.

images.subject: Waterite filter control valve
images.hard: EXIF-rotated 90°; the model is HANDWRITTEN in ballpoint on a printed blank

fieldNotes.model: Handwritten across two lines: 'FZ110' over '1054PB'. Legible here. Compare IMG_0029/IMG_0030, where the same hand is not.

images.subject: Waterite softener control valve
images.hard: EXIF-rotated 90°; handwritten model, smudged; the label is scuffed and the ink has worn

fieldNotes.model: GENUINE ABSTENTION — the important one in this set. The handwriting reads as something like 'WDBT' over 'PC1', but the first token is genuinely ambiguous between several letter shapes and the ink is worn. A confident 'WDBT PC1' here is a guess wearing a transcription's clothes. Unknown is the correct answer; the concierge types it in or carries it to the next visit.

images.subject: Same valve as IMG_0029, second attempt from further back
images.hard: EXIF-rotated 90°; flatter light, so the handwriting is WORSE here than in IMG_0029 despite being the same label

fieldNotes.model: GENUINE ABSTENTION. Two photos of one plate, neither of which yields the model — the pair proves the abstention is a property of the label, not of one unlucky shot. Both must abstain independently; neither may borrow the other's reading.
fieldNotes.serial: Printed, not handwritten, and legible in both frames. A plate can be half-readable, and the honest output says which half.

images.subject: Liberty Pumps Pro380 sewage pump
images.hard: the darkest image in the set, EXIF-rotated 180°, and a deep shadow swallows the top of the data plate including the start of the model number

fieldNotes.model: GENUINE ABSTENTION. Two candidate strings compete and neither is readable as a model. The data plate's model field trails off into shadow, showing only '...82LE41'; separately, a product badge reads 'Pro380'. Completing the plate value from Liberty's catalogue, or promoting the badge into the model field, are both inference. Unknown.
fieldNotes.serial: 'SERIAL CODE: B10208434' is legible despite the shadow.

images.subject: Geo-Flo circulator pump
images.hard: cropped and downscaled unlike the rest of the set; text is moulded into black plastic rather than printed, so it reads by relief only

fieldNotes.serial: GENUINE ABSTENTION. The plate carries a part number (P/N 52722357P1) and a production code (PC 2432) but no serial. A P/N is not a serial, and reporting one as the other is the failure mode this entry exists to catch.

notes: TWELVE OF FIFTEEN ARE EXIF-ROTATED. Orientation=6 on twelve, Orientation=3 on IMG_0033, none on the other two. Photo viewers apply the tag; reading the raw bytes does not. Anything that feeds these to a model must normalise orientation first or every plate arrives sideways — which turns a legibility test into an accidental test of reading upside-down text.
FOR DAVID — three things to confirm before this file is treated as ground truth:
1. IMG_0009 is my pick for 'the one that isn't a nameplate at all'. It is the only whole-unit shot with no data plate in frame. Confirm, or name the one you meant.

2. You said 'a couple that are genuinely illegible'. On my reading, no image in this set is illegible end to end — but five have individual fields that genuinely cannot be read: the model on IMG_0029, IMG_0030 and IMG_0033, and the serial on IMG_0008, IMG_0020 and Untitled.jpg (those three plates carry no serial at all). If you intended a whole image to be unreadable, tell me which and I will look again — I would rather re-examine than record an expectation that flatters the reading.

4. KNOWN GAP — the whole-image abstention path has no fixture yet. Two more photos are
       coming (something genuinely blurred, and a plate in the dark at a steep angle). Until
       they land, no entry in this set expects `abstains: true` on a photo that IS a nameplate,
       so the state where extraction runs and returns nothing at all is exercised only by unit
       tests with a stubbed model, never against a real image.

3. Worth knowing how I read them: full size, on a strong model, with time. The fast tier that will actually run this in production sees them at lower resolution and will do worse. That asymmetry is the point of the file — expected.json records what the plate SAYS, so a weak reading fails visibly instead of quietly becoming the record.
